title: What is one customer worth?
principle: A customer is worth the margin on all their future buys.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a famous study from 1990. Two researchers, Frederick Reichheld and Earl Sasser, studied service businesses such as banks. They asked one question: what happens to profit when a few more customers stay?

screens.prompt: Imagine a business keeps 5 more customers out of every 100 each year. What do you think they estimated for its profit?
screens.why: They estimated profits could rise by 25% to 85%, depending on the business. Five more customers out of 100 doesn't sound like much. But a customer who stays keeps buying, year after year.

screens.title: Customer lifetime value
screens.text: The money one customer brings you over all their years is called customer lifetime value, or LTV. Count the margin you keep, not the price they pay. The sum: margin on each order × orders a year × years they stay.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Those studies looked at banks, but your best customers work the same way. It's June. One family has ordered from you for three years: four birthday cakes every year. Each ₹850 cake leaves you ₹450.

screens.prompt: A family orders 4 cakes a year. Each leaves you ₹450. If they stay 5 more years, what's their lifetime value from now?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹450 × 4 cakes = ₹1,800 a year, and 5 years makes ₹9,000. That family isn't an ₹850 order. It's ₹9,000 of profit, if you keep them happy.

wrong.a: ₹1,800 is one year: ₹450 × 4. They stay 5 years, so ₹1,800 × 5 = ₹9,000.
wrong.c: You used the price: ₹850 × 4 × 5. Lifetime value counts what you keep: ₹450 × 4 × 5 = ₹9,000.

screens.text: The café deal leaves you ₹1,750 a week. Over 50 weeks a year: ₹1,750 × 50 = ___ a year, and 2 years make ___.
screens.why: Right. ₹1,750 × 50 = ₹87,500 a year, and 2 years make ₹1,75,000. That café isn't one order. It's your biggest customer.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six ideas. For each one, tell me: does it raise lifetime value, or only today's sale?

items.text: A message a week before each child's birthday
₹100 off for anyone, this Sunday only
A bigger cake at the same price, just this once
Keep a note of each family's birthdays and orders
A festival sale banner on your menu

screens.why: Good. The first kind makes families stay and order again: a reminder, their favourite flavour, knowing their dates. The second kind helps one sale and then stops.

screens.prompt: You think of a ₹400 trial cake, which leaves you nothing, to win new families. When does it make sense?

options.label: When most of them come back at ₹850
When it brings lots of first orders
When other bakers are cheaper than you

screens.why: Exactly. You met this in Unit 3: a cheap first offer pays only if buyers return at full price. The trial cake earns nothing. Lifetime value is what pays for it.

wrong.b: Lots of ₹0 orders still make ₹0. Remember Unit 3: a cheap first offer pays only if buyers come back at full price.
wrong.c: Then you'd be fighting on price. Remember Unit 3: a cheap first offer pays only if buyers come back at the full ₹850.

screens.setup: It's mid-June, 3 pm. A family who orders 4 cakes a year calls, upset: today's birthday cake arrived squashed. Baking a fresh one costs you ₹400 and two hours. The party starts at 7 pm.
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Say sorry and give ₹100 off their next cake
options.outcome: They have a party tonight and a squashed cake. They thank you coldly. Next birthday, they order from someone else. You saved ₹400 and lost about ₹9,000 over the next five years.
options.why: You protected today's ₹400 and lost a family worth about ₹9,000.
options.better: Bake a fresh cake now and deliver it before 7 pm, free.

options.label: Bake a fresh cake now and deliver it free
options.outcome: The new cake arrives at 6:30 pm. The mother sends a photo of the candles and thanks you in the colony group. They keep ordering. You spent ₹400 to keep a family worth about ₹9,000.
options.why: You judged the cost against the family's lifetime value, not against one cake.

options.label: Refund the full ₹850 and say sorry
options.outcome: They're glad to get the money back, but they buy a shop cake for tonight. Next time, they're not sure about you. You're ₹850 down and may lose the family.
options.why: A refund is fair, but it didn't save the party, and the party was what they paid for.
options.better: Bake a fresh cake now and deliver it before 7 pm, free.

screens.text: A customer is worth the ___ on all their ___ buys, not just the first.
screens.why: Exactly. Reichheld and Sasser estimated that keeping a few more customers could raise profits a lot. Your squashed-cake family is worth about ₹9,000, not ₹850.

summary: Customer lifetime value (LTV): the margin one customer brings you over all their years.
LTV = margin on each order × orders a year × years they stay.
When a problem comes up, compare its cost with the customer's lifetime value, not one order.

cards.front: A family orders 4 cakes a year at ₹450 margin and stays 5 years. LTV?
Lifetime value counts which number from each order?
cards.back: Count what you keep, not what they pay.

cards.front: Fixing a regular customer's problem costs ₹400. They're worth ₹9,000 over the years. Fix it?
cards.back: Compare the cost with lifetime value, not one order.

sources.label: Reichheld and Sasser, Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services (Harvard Business Review, Sep–Oct 1990)
Ipsos, Shattering myths about customer loyalty (quotes the 25% to 85% finding)
Reichheld, Here's the truth about customer retention (American Banker, 1991)
